utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before we bring in the witness, we would like the opportunity to respond to the concerns you raised at the close of the session yesterday. Thank you. The Prosecution believes that the submissions of the appellant and his current counsel in this matter, as well as the testimony of Mr. Tadic himself thus far, go beyond addressing the bare facts of whether Mr. Vujin's alleged actions amount to contempt. They've also raised the issue of possible prejudice to the appellant caused by those actions. These claims were raised shortly after the denial of the Rule 115 motion by the Appeals Chamber. As a result of that denial, the Prosecution believes that the complaints of the appellant and his counsel are in part designed to raise the spectre that Mr. Vujin's misconduct acted towards the prejudice of the appellant and, therefore, would form the case for corrective actions by the Appeals Chamber or, more simply, could provide a second bite of the apple. The examination of Mr. Tadic which we are conducting is a response to the posture of these proceedings as created by the appellant and his counsel, and we feel bound to test that posture. Our questions are intended to deal not only with the facts regarding Mr. Vujin's misconduct, but also to establish that Mr. Tadic was a willing participant in that misconduct and was happy to go along with the submission of false evidence because it was all potentially exculpatory. It is only since the Rule 115 motion did not go his way that he again abandoned his Defence counsel and is trying to use the situation to his advantage. Given the discussions in the appeal hearing last week relating to the Defence counsel request that the Appeals Chamber leave open the possibility of consideration of additional matters that might develop at this hearing, the Prosecution believes it is necessary to address those issues in order to establish that there has been no showing of prejudice to the appellant and that there is no justification for any further consideration of additional matters related to his appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keegan. Mr. Abell, would you like to respond very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be my submission that we have to be -- I'm so sorry. It would be my submission that we have to be very careful here. The starting point is: What are the particular proceedings that we are engaged in at the moment, and what is the status of Mr. Tadic in those proceedings? To state the obvious, the individual who is accused, if I can use that word, although not in the dock, in the contempt proceedings is Mr. Vujin. The status of Mr. Tadic is that he is a witness. He is a witness who is on the Appeals Chamber's list of witnesses in relation to the contempt motion. He can give relevant evidence as to certain aspects which touch upon the five allegations against Mr. Vujin, and he can give evidence which is supportive of those charges in the sense that it tends to show the context in which the allegations were said to be committed and the motive underlying them. I am not here -- I am separate counsel from counsel representing Mr. Tadic as an appellant. He does not come here today or yesterday as an appellant but as a witness. If, and I cannot say because I do not represent him in the appeal, if any consequences whatsoever flow from these proceedings, it would be my submission that they would need to be addressed by his counsel in the appeal and that it would be when this Court -- when Your Honours are sitting in the appeal, if there is to be any more of it at all, that any considerations flowing from today's proceedings should follow. In other words, if I can put it another way, these proceedings shouldn't, and I say this with great respect to my friends who prosecute, these proceedings shouldn't be used as a platform in which to attempt to show that Mr. Tadic is seeking a second bite of a cherry or seeking to improve or better his position in order to perhaps influence his chances that he may or may not have on the major appeal. What I am saying, I'm agreeing with Your Honours, but we should endeavour to restrict ourselves to questions which have relevance in the light of the allegations that today's proceedings are all about. In other words, what goes directly to those allegations and what goes to those allegations in terms of motive or supporting evidence. Of course, the Prosecution, if they wish, can cross-examine Mr. Tadic as to credibility, but really only in that context. I hope that wasn't too long an answer, but obviously I'm concerned that we don't confuse the separate hearings which are taking place. That is, in my submission, the starting point, and that is the key to the answer to the response raised by the Prosecution, unless I can assist further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, would you like to intervene on the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. My comment, when I received the orders charging me that I had been obstructing the work of this Tribunal to the detriment of Mr. Tadic, I will refrain from commenting because I believe the Prosecution is right, and the questioning by the representative, the counsel for Mr. Tadic of yesterday, represents an attempt to gain information which could possibly have an effect on a more favourable outcome which I, as former counsel for Mr. Tadic, would want. However, following the questioning of yesterday, and in view that questions were asked about periods which are outside of the period during which I am charged -- with the activities that I'm charged with, and partially it is a result of imprecise claims against me, because from all the material that I have received, it is clear that these are only certain actions in question, and I would like for these proceedings to finish with that, for it to be established whether I committed these actions or not. For these reasons, I ask that the Court allows this, since the questioning of Tadic, in a way, has been imposed. Then in the future, to limit these proceedings only to those actions that I have been charged with. I also believe that once the questioning of Mr. Tadic is completed, he be not allowed to remain in the courtroom, in view of the fact that he is a witness, and he, therefore, should not be in the courtroom while other witnesses are being questioned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, all interested parties have been heard, as is the proper course. It will be remembered that yesterday the bench had occasion once and perhaps twice to intervene on this point and to call attention to a distinction between the two sets of proceedings. It was pointed out that these proceedings are limited to five concrete and specific allegations and that although it may occasionally be difficult to say that something is not quite relevant in the sense of being dead on the point, still one could sometimes, indeed, often say that something is only subliminally or marginally relevant. I would ask all parties to confine themselves to the five concrete allegations, and if they go outside of those allegations, please be careful to remember the distinction between the two sets of proceedings lest it be said, and said with justification, that an attempt is being made to use these proceedings to lay the groundwork for an application in the other. That should happen, if it happens, only accidentally and not with deliberation or purpose. So the ruling of the Chamber is that as questions have been asked by Mr. Abell on matters which, in the view of the bench, are not fully circumscribed by the five concrete and specific allegations, Mr. Keegan is entitled to ask counter-questions on those points. I will ask him to be diligent and careful, to make sure that his efforts are brief and perfectly manageable by the Tribunal both in this case and in the other. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could bring in Mr. Tadic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you will still be under oath which you took yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. What I would like to begin with is going back to the letters which you wrote to Mr. Vujin, which we began discussing yesterday. If I could have those letters provided to the witness, please. These are copies of the letters that we have been referring to, Mr. Tadic, if you feel the need to refer to them as a result of my questions. Yesterday we began with the letter dated 4 March, 1997, which would be the letter marked with the number 274. That appears to be the first letter which you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, I rather think Mr. Abell wishes to say something. Do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I was only trying to indicate to one of the clerks that if there was a spare copy for me as well it would be helpful. I wasn't trying to disturb Your Honours, I was trying to do it discreetly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation, Mr. Abell. Mr. Keegan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That appears to be the first letter that you wrote to Mr. Vujin after you decided to retain him again for your case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know which letter you're referring to, what number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It should have a sticker on the top, a green sticker on the top with the number 274, and the date of the letter is 4 March, 1997.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but I only have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Apparently that was the only version provided in the record. In that letter which was written almost two months before the decision in your case, you write, at the page marked 274: "I suppose that the Tribunal will find me guilty for some acts from the indictment and that I must have prepared evidence to assure the higher Chamber who lied before this Tribunal." At the time that you specifically brought Mr. Vujin back into your case, you at that time believed you were going to be convicted, and that you would need some new evidence to try and convince the Appeals Chamber that your victims had lied during the trial; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that was one of the assumptions, but I mostly received assurances that I would not be convicted of the gravest acts, and Mr. Wladimiroff even told my family that he expected I would be declared innocent for the gravest breaches. So that was one of my assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You also, in that letter, list some questions that you want Mr. Vujin to provide you concrete answers to because that would directly affect your further steps in the case. Those questions include how many witnesses that he could call before the Tribunal, the names of those witnesses, and the necessary conditions for him to be successfully engaged in the presentation of new evidence. When you brought Mr. Vujin back into your case then, is it not correct that you had very specific ideas of what you expected him to do and what evidence you wanted to bring forward?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: These questions are the result of my meetings with Mr. Ambassador who had direct contacts with Mr. Vujin for several months before this was written, and this is the product of information based on which he told me that Vujin was ready, that he had witnesses. We did not talk about the manner this would be done and how it would be done, but Mr. Wladimiroff did tell me this was important and, in accordance with that, I really wanted to know what was it that he had available to him. So these are my thoughts, but I wasn't sure really in what way and when he would be able to use them. This is something that Vujin was offering to me from '96. He was offering me witnesses, and he said that he had them definitely, but I could not have seen them during the regular proceedings and, obviously, I did not have the opportunity to see them during these proceedings, but I believe that now if he took part in the team again that these witnesses would be available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When the evidence that you were looking for did not turn out the way you wanted, when people did not line up to support you as you thought they should, you yourself took part in the fabrication of the evidence that you believed necessary to support your claims; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Then how do you explain the statements from Radic and Zigic?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was not my idea. Just by pure chance, it happened that Mr. Radic was here, and I always insisted that these statements be taken out in the field. However, obviously this was something that Mr. Vujin avoided. I was not satisfied with Mr. Radic's statement because it was obvious that he was lying because he was avoiding saying that he was the head of the shift of the guards. So I didn't know in which way this statement would be used by Mr. Vujin, whether it would be submitted. I did not have any influence on what things would be submitted to the Court and which ones would not be, so many things I was not aware of. I didn't know what was happening in the relations between the Tribunal and Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When that statement was submitted by Mr. Vujin to the Appeals Chamber, did you or your other counsel ever ask that that statement be removed from the filings or not be considered by the Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know that. I said that I wasn't sure what was directly submitted to the Court and what were the things that I received from Mr. Vujin. I don't know what Mr. Livingston had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to the letter dated 12 June, 1997. That would be the statement with the green sticker on the top marked "271." Addressing this issue of what you knew and didn't know about the pleadings being submitted in your case, in that letter, you're giving specific directions to Mr. Vujin on how the arguments on your sentence should be divided. In that letter, you also indicate that prior to the hearing, Mr. Vujin should go to Republika Srpska to confirm the presence of witnesses before the Tribunal and discuss their role before the ICTY. So you were, in fact, specifically aware not only of the pleadings being prepared but also of the substance of negotiations between your counsel and the authorities of Republika Srpska; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly you mean in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Well, I refer you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, I'm reading your question on the screen. I think it extends to something like 13 lines or more. I wonder if you would find any virtue in a little more brevity so that you might, in the course of that, facilitate comprehension by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Isn't it true that on the first page of that letter, you are specifically giving directions to your counsel about a trip to Banja Luka and the specific reasons that he is supposed to go there for? In the English translation, it's the last paragraph of the first page and moving on to the second page.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll move on. On the second page of that document, do you specifically state: "... that the solution of my case must be approached in the way in which we agreed at our last meeting"? That would be the sentence that's underlined on the second page there.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't find it, but would you ask your question regarding this sentence? I can't find it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Excuse me for intervening --

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please tell me how the sentence starts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us hear Mr. Abell, perhaps, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting and perhaps putting my friend off his stride, but one of the problems is that I believe the documents that Mr. Tadic is being asked about are in English. That makes it extremely difficult for this witness who has a little English but only a smattering. It may be difficult for him.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, I do have a version in Serbian. I have a version in Serbian, but it's a copy so I can't really see where I am. I don't have anything underlined in my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: (Obscured by interpretation) ... not on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please tell me how the sentence begins?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. The sentence begins, "Besides this, I think that the solution of my case must be approached in the way in which we agreed in our last meeting," and the last part of that sentence would be underlined.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In that letter on that same page, the very next section, you also direct that all communications with the ICTY should go only through Mr. Vujin, and you specifically state that you do not want too much of a close relationship between the members of his team and the Prosecution or the Tribunal in general. Do you see that provision?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is the result of the various suggestions that I was given at that time, so that I expressed one of my opinions to Mr. Vujin; yes, that's correct. Secondly, at that time, there was a problem because Mr. Kostic used to receive the Tribunal's mail, so there were misunderstandings. He would receive the information first and then Vujin himself would receive the information later. Then for this reason, Vujin asked that everything went through him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So that would explain then why the last sentence of that letter is that if any of the assistants have any questions, they could come to you for an explanation as to why you were directing this to happen?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Isn't this letter, in fact, a clear indication that you were exerting control over the preparation of the appeal in your case?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I tried to have control all of the time; yes, that's true. However, it's a different story of how much my counsel took into account my requests. Mostly, they took into consideration some not so important things, but everything basically came down to bringing eyewitnesses before the Tribunal and also important documents that I knew existed in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Moving to the next letter of 15 July, 1997, which should have the green sticker marked "252" on the top, this letter then would have been written a couple of weeks after your sentence had been delivered and the notice of appeal filed in your case; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Which number, 250?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It should be number 252.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The point of this letter is that you disagreed with Mr. Vujin with the appeal basis as listed, and you directed him to change the appeal documents and further to disclose this letter to the public and to the Tribunal; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: If that's what it says here, then it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you not also in this letter tell Mr. Vujin to warn the authorities in Yugoslavia and in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin never complied with that direction, did he?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, the essential points, I considered that he did not. But some of the questions that I asked him were the subject of my deliberations and what Mr. Livingston and Mr. Kostic advised because at that time, I had a feeling that there was a sort of competition, rivalry between them. Everybody put forward different ideas, and then I tried to present this in some way. Mr. Vujin was the leader of the Defence team, and therefore I considered it appropriate that he hear my opinion, which was, of course, not binding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So neither Mr. Vujin nor, in fact, Mr. Livingston ever took your direction and changed the Defence submissions to indicate that the Defence agreed with Judge McDonald's dissenting opinion in the Tadic decision that, in fact, there was an international armed conflict in Bosnia, did they?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they never. Mr. Livingston explained to me that that could not have an effect on my judgement and the discussions within the Trial Chamber, but Mr. Vujin was against this because he knew my essential problem, that it was in my interest to present before this Tribunal the eyewitnesses of the events for which I was found guilty or charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: They also did not disclose this letter as you directed, did they?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: They never did. I don't mean the majority, but this type of communication with the public, I did not ask for of Mr. Livingston because he said to begin with that he would give no interviews and that that was the code of conduct of British lawyers. However, Vujin would frequently talk to the members of the press, and he had occasion to do so, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, the bench has said that matters outside of the three concrete allegations having been raised, you are entitled to explore that territory, but the more you do so, the more the impression crystallises with us that these matters are remote from the specific allegations which have been made, and I would urge you once again to try to bear that consideration in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you yourself never disclosed this letter either, did you?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that because it would have affected the cooperation you were getting from Republika Srpska for the production of evidence from individuals such as Zigic and Radic?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't think about those individuals, but I personally considered that if the authorities of the Republika Srpska, in general terms, did not wish to cooperate where my personal problems are concerned, then I considered that it was not in my interest to think about acts which go towards accepting Mrs. McDonald's position. As I say, I didn't think that this could cause particular harm to me personally. Even if it did, I thought that I had already been punished by the very fact that I was not able to prove my -- that various structures prevented me from proving my innocence before this Tribunal. They celebrated the judgement there, and when the appeal was rejected that was a matter of celebration for them over there, so that those were my positions vis-à-vis the authorities in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If that is the case, Mr. Tadic, then why in your next letter of October 4, 1997 did you, in fact, support Mr. Vujin as your lead counsel stating that: "Because of all the matters we've discussed earlier, I believe now is the last and right moment to unify your previous and present work," and at the same time complain about the work of Mr. Vujin --

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Which letter are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This would have the number "201" on the top.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Which letter? Which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It will have the green sticker on the top that says "201." It's in your own handwriting and it's dated 4 October, 1997.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Aren't your statements regarding both your counsel in this letter a device which you used to play your attorneys off against one another to achieve the ends which you desired?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that it is quite the reverse. I always insisted upon that cooperation, and I asked the two men to cooperate. On one occasion, I made Mr. Livingston travel to Belgrade. I asked him to do so and he agreed to. However, in the situation in which I found myself, it was difficult to find myself positioned between two lawyers, because their strategies were quite different and the way in which they worked in the field was quite different. So I didn't know what to do. Very often they would not be on speaking terms. When I talked to Mr. Vujin, I would gain the impression that Mr. Livingston wasn't working well, but when we parted, I would realise that that was not the case and that something was amiss, and that Mr. Livingston was indeed doing everything in his power to come by the proper evidence. Mr. Vujin and his secretary that you mentioned a few days ago, said that he wasn't free to work in the field and that Livingston was an impediment to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In your final letter to Mr. Vujin, dated 16 November, 1997, you give him very specific directions as to how to complete the submissions on the new evidence for your appeal, do you not?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I see the letter. The question of the long-term work that I had with Mr. Livingston linked to attempts to arrive at eyewitnesses and written evidence in the territory of the Republika Srpska. Mr. Livingston, of course, wished to have agreement from Mr. Vujin, as the lead counsel. So it would be impossible to get an order without him. So that is what I did, in keeping with the agreement that I had reached with Mr. Livingston, that is to say, it was a sort of rough portion of the way in which his deliberations went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Isn't it true that at that point you were dissatisfied with all of the efforts because they were not turning out the way you were hoping or dreaming that they were? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there was always this problem of the lack of co-operation between them. I wanted to have a meeting between the two in Belgrade. It was difficult. Mr. Vujin quite simply said that he liked to work alone, independently, and to co-operate with our people. That was the problem. That was always the problem, the underlying problem. I did not want to lose my foreign lawyer, because I knew what they were doing in the field. In that period too, Mr. John Livingston had a lot of evidence that he came by himself and that he never let Mr. Vujin see. He wished to check it out and to do it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that why then, in the letter of 2 February 1998, you criticise Mr. Livingston very harshly and demand that he return all the personal documents and letters that you had given him, and that you further direct him to give all directions on his future work through Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a great problem. Mr. Vujin did always protest with respect to that, and it was a technical problem as well, because most of the documents that I had in my room I had to send to Mr. Livingston. So I had no more documents in my room and wasn't able to follow what was going on, what was happening. That is why I wanted to see what was going on, all the more so as all the preparatory documents were written and sometimes given to me to have a look at them in English. So very often I wasn't able to understand the material submitted to me, and I couldn't grasp what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After you sent this letter did Mr. Livingston then begin to toe the line, as it were, or follow the directions that you gave him?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: For the most part, yes, but he would always ask to study the documents and then return them. It was a period in which it was very -- it was a very difficult period for me, and further co-operation with Mr. Livingston was brought into question. There was pressure on me to cease that co-operation, but I consulted some members of my family and we considered that that would be a great pity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You say that this was a difficult period, that time was a difficult period for you. Is that because you believed that as a result of your significant assistance to the Serb cause in Kozarac and Prijedor that you were entitled to support from the authorities but you weren't getting the support that you thought you were entitled to?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: People laugh at that kind of observation, people living in the Prijedor municipality. They are laughing because I have experienced the tragedy that I have experienced, whereas they are at liberty and walk freely around the Prijedor municipality. I never had the support of those authorities. The very fact that my family was expelled in April 1992, they have never succeeded in returning to Prijedor, my property remains over there, everything is empty, and I never had any understanding from the authorities there. If somebody tried to help me, it was individuals who, for the most part, tried to help me through contacts with the foreign lawyers, because they did not trust the lawyers from the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You say that your family was expelled in April 1992 and they've never succeeded in returning? Who then is running the Cafe Neplan in Kozarac and who has been running it since the fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, how does this have any bearing on the five allegations presented in the Court's motion? May I remind you, as I would remind all parties, these proceedings have been initiated by the Appeals Chamber itself. We've invited Mr. Tadic and yourself to give assistance to the Chamber, but we do not have here a roving inquiry into matters not reasonably connected with the allegations. So while it is true that questions have been asked which might be considered as going outside of the circumference of the allegations which have been presented, while you're entitled, therefore, to deal with that area of inquiry, please, may I counsel you to be as brief and as economical as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will move on. This, in fact, was obviously something that hadn't come up, but where a witness is making a blatantly false statement under oath to the Trial Chamber, we believe it goes to credibility and that's why I was challenging that submission, but I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, yesterday you referred to Mr. Vujin's conduct during your interview with the ICTY. You alleged that Mr. Vujin told you not to speak of certain individuals, that is, people in positions of authority in Prijedor or to discuss certain topics and that as a result, you were unable to be completely open during the course of that interview. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I recall that, but you asked me a moment ago with regard to my cafe, the question about my cafe. My cafe never worked after May 1992. It has been greatly destroyed and it is not working today. Nor do any of the members of my family live in the part of the house that belonged to me. As far as your second question is concerned, I did not say that I was not honest. I was honest and frank in trying to answer the questions that were asked me during my first interview, but I said that I felt that I was under a certain amount of pressure because at times I did not know how to behave. I had never talked to the representatives of the International Tribunal before that occasion and, of course, I asked Vujin what I should do, how I should behave. I asked Mr. Wladimiroff that too. Mr. Wladimiroff gave me some advice and Mr. Vujin did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You also stated that during the interview itself, Mr. Vujin directed you to watch him and that he would tell you or signal you when you should not answer questions. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if I put it that way. I don't know if I said that I shouldn't answer. That wasn't the concrete agreement. We did not actually decide that he would tell me when not to speak, but I just know that he told me that if I watched him, I would know how to behave. I can't quote his exact words at the time, but he told me to look at him and that I would get guidance from him as to how to behave. If you look at the tape, then you will know whether that is so or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You specifically mentioned yesterday the issue of the crisis staff and indicated that you were instructed not to discuss the crisis staff. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: To be aware of what I say about the crisis staff and how I use the term "camp." I didn't say everything yesterday. There was a lot of that kind of thing, but that is what was most objectionable to the people from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The record of your interview is part of the record of the appeal in this case and is, therefore, available to this Chamber. It is quite voluminous. In that record of interview, you give an extensive explanation of your alibi, your whereabouts, and who the witnesses were that could support that to explain why you were not guilty of any of the crimes alleged. Given the nature of that record of interview, your responses, what evidence, what indication can you point to that you were under any undue pressure or given any particular directions not to co-operate?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was advice given me before the interview started. Nobody knew what questions would be raised, nor could anybody assume what was going to be asked, and I myself did not know what I was going to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said yesterday that as a result of the pressure you felt, you, in fact, asked Mr. Wladimiroff not to inform Mr. Vujin about the second session of your record of interview. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In comparing the second session to the first session, there's virtually no distinction between the nature, scope, or extent of your responses. So what, in fact, then was the change?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I felt myself to be under pressure. I wasn't able to talk freely. You or whoever interviewed me at the time was free to ask whatever they wanted to ask, but many of the questions were not asked then, questions which might have been important at the time, so that it remained open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that after your interview, your family experienced difficulties because both Karadzic and Mladic found out about the interview and did not like what you said about the crisis staff. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why is it then is that neither you nor any members of your family have ever given any indication of these difficulties in any of your prior statements or submissions related to this matter or any other matter before this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I told my lawyers this, and they knew more about that than I did myself because they contacted with the members of my family more. Mr. Wladimiroff, and Steven Kay, and Orie, and later on Mr. Livingston as well, considered that my family ought not to continue to live in the Prijedor municipality. Not because of the fact that our neighbours were returning, but because of the development of the investigation that was under way. There were a number of dangerous people living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Livingston discuss whether the fact that your family had had direct consequences as a result of your interview, did you discuss whether that should be a part of your submissions in regard to Mr. Vujin's misconduct?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't know that I would be in a situation where I would have to testify publicly ever. At the beginning, I informed the competent authorities, that is to say, I asked for a change of attorney. As the attorneys would change several times, it was impossible. I had to tell the representative of the registry why I asked for a change. When I explained that reasons existed for that, that is how things unfolded. I did not think about -- I never thought that it would end in this way, nor was it my wish to do so. I'm sorry to be in this kind of situation, because I know that many members of my family will never feel safe in the Republika Srpska-Yugoslavia area, and probably myself too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, your testimony has been that the reason that your family will never feel safe again is because Mr. Vujin disclosed the contents of your interview. My question was: Did you and Mr. Livingston ever discuss whether that impact should be part of your submissions on these allegations of Mr. Vujin's misconduct?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. There was no mention of that. I don't know whether there was any mention of that. I didn't know which direction this would go, whether it was showing respect for the Court or not. I don't know what you mean actually. My family, in 1996, following the advice of Mr. Wladimiroff, tried to solve its status in Prijedor, and he undertook efforts to settle their status, but it didn't progress. Then they tried to solve this in another way. I didn't want to and neither do I want to now to involve the problems of my family in this discussion. You asked me about the problems of my brothers. I know that my brothers do have problems in Prijedor. They always had problems here. I never brought that up before this Tribunal, but many members of my family and my brothers distance themselves from me, precisely because they consider that everything happening here is not worthy of the problems that they are having to face in Prijedor. My younger brother was taken into custody. So was my brother Ljuba. Those are the problems they have to face living there, but I do not want to enter into polemics about that, and I don't want the Tribunal to discuss things like that. I don't think that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, yesterday you indicated that Mr. Vujin has moved people from Prijedor to Serbia to protect them. Are you prepared to tell us who those people are and where they are?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I know for certain that Mr. Saponja was in Zemun. This was discovered by Mr. Livingston, through some of his connections in Omarska. Later, when where we found out where he was, Mr. Vujin transferred him to a different address and told me that he was his priority and he wanted to get him a job. Mr. Danicic is in Montenegro under a different name. Most of them received new identity cards and passports. I know that. I don't have any proof, but I have information that Mr. Vujin took part in all of that. I know what his authorities, what his powers were in that in order to get them passports very quickly. My brother Ljubomir told me that. Mr. Dusan Jankovic also bought a house in Novi Sad. He's residing in Novi Sad. In order for their safety, they mostly move between Serbia and Prijedor. Mr. Milomir Stakic, who was the commander of the crisis staff of the municipality of Prijedor, after the arrest of Kovacevic, fled the same day, and allegedly he's on specialisation in Belgrade. He's staying there. He's being financed by the municipality of Prijedor while he's staying in Belgrade. Dusan Knezevic is also in Belgrade, and I know that they all meet in Mr. Vujin's office. He told me that himself. Occasionally they come to Republika Srpska, but mostly the majority of those people who gave the statements, they have cited the wrong dates and wrong places of where the statements were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When did Mr. Vujin tell you that Milomir Stakic, Dusan Knezevic, and others meet immediate in his office in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but it did happen that I would call him on the telephone and then he would say, "Well, these people are here. Let's talk at another time." I don't know exactly what date that was. As far as Stakic is concerned, I heard from my wife, who used to work in the medical centre in Prijedor, and she's well-informed, that he's being financed -- his stay in Belgrade is being financed by the Prijedor Hospital and the municipality of Prijedor. She also was able to see a fax in which he demands that they send him 5.000 German Marks urgently. He also has changed his appearance. I have heard that a few of them have had plastic surgery. Not only those persons who were accused but also those who think they may be accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Other than Mr. Saponja, and we'll come back to him, what information or evidence do you have that Mr. Vujin is directly linked to the relocation of any of these other people that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Livingston found out the telephone number of his residence in Zemun, and he spoke with his aunt or somebody and she said, "He's at work right now." Later, Mr. Vujin told me this part about getting him a job. The problem was in the fact that I was not happy with the statement of that gentleman. On one occasion, Mr. Vujin brought Mr. Saponja's statement. He didn't say anything. Then Mr. Vujin, the second time he met with him in his office, allegedly, he said that he would take a new statement, and I had gone over these statements recently and saw that the first page was as the first page of the first statement, and there was a little part added at the end. So I looked at the dates, and then later I really couldn't tell what was actually said and at what date. I know that he had taken a videotape from him later, but I don't know anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Let's follow up on Mr. Saponja. What you testified earlier was that Mr. Vujin specifically relocated him and gave him a different address in Serbia and got him a job. What information or evidence do you have to verify that, not that Mr. Vujin contacted him and took a statement but that he relocated him and provided him with a job?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: He told me that when we were talking about work for my wife, and he told me personally that his priority right now was to see to Mr. Saponja, to find him a new job and an apartment. He even told me that he had found an apartment for him, but I don't know if he had found him a job at that time. As far as his stay was concerned there, he had changed his address. This is what Vujin told me personally. I don't know where he is living now, but I know that Mr. Livingston has the telephone number of his previous residence and where he was previously working. This is known to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, other than Mr. Saponja, you mentioned several other individuals. What information or evidence do you have that Mr. Vujin had any part in their relocation, the providing of new identities, or any other assistance to help them avoid detection in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as Mr. Jankovic is concerned, I think that it is not hard to check who took part in the purchase and the contract for the purchase of the house in Novi Sad. This is something that I found out from a member of my family. As far as Mr. Radanovic, Ciga Radanovic, former mayor and the head of the paramilitary group which took part in the conflict in Kozarac, he was staying in Hotel Yugoslavia. I got some of this information from some members of my family, from some people from Omarska. These people, you need to know that they contact their friends in Prijedor. They are always interested in how my proceedings are coming along before the Tribunal, so I know about all of these -- that they receive information, that they are following what is happening. Occasionally, they even go back to Prijedor. But mostly they have enough money because they made money dishonestly during the war, so most of them are able to stay in these places. As far as my information tells me, Mr. Vujin mostly participated in providing them with a place to live, assistance with accommodation in Belgrade and the surrounding towns, and also in the issuance of identity cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You also said yesterday that there were seven or eight important witnesses for your case that Mr. Vujin failed to take meaningful statements from. Is it the case that he took any type of statement from those people, and if so, where are they?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: One of the key persons who we know for certain could have testified regarding the killing of the police officers in Kozarac is Mr. Jankovic, Dusan Jankovic, who at that time was the chief of police in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, we will suspend at this time until 11.30 when we will resume and go on until maybe ten minutes to one. Would you have much more, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I have one other question if you would like to finish it before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We would be delighted to facilitate you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In the submissions filed in this case, Mr. Tadic, and in your testimony yesterday, you referred to misconduct by two other attorneys who practice before this Tribunal, Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Tosic in regards to their assistance to Mr. Vujin. What evidence or information do you have regarding any specific misconduct by those two attorneys?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Tosic was present in Prijedor during the attempt to implement the order, and he was actively included in the contacts and the investigation conducted by Mr. Vujin. I believe that he should not have had access to documents from my case because he is the Defence counsel for Mr. Zigic. So I don't think that was okay. I think that this had a negative impact in this sense. He was also present during the visit of the delegation when he heard what his client Zigic said about what the strategy of Mr. Vujin is, not to allow any new persons to be arrested and for none of the people from here to leave. In that case, they felt that nothing would be achieved. I feel that he should have distanced himself from such statements if he did not support them, and if he did support them, I don't believe that this is all right. Besides that, I think that he took part in the transfer of Mr. Ratkovic from Foca to Banja Luka because he heard that every time Mr. Vujin or Mr. Livingston tried to interview him, Mr. Tosic was always represented as the Defence counsel of those people who were supposed to be interviewed. We didn't know whether these people would say anything significant or not. This is an organised group who knows exactly what it's doing and who it is protecting in the municipality of Prijedor. I don't believe that they protected me and I don't believe they are protecting the other people who are here. I think that they are exclusively trying to protect people who are free; they are much more important. They are still carrying out important functions in the municipality of Prijedor and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keegan. The Appeals Chamber will now suspend until 25 minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by taking on myself the responsibility of the delay. There were circumstances beyond my control. I ask your indulgence. Now we would invite Mr. Vujin to examine the witness. Mr. Vujin, I think you recognise, as experienced counsel, that there was general agreement with the position which you took, that the distinction had to be drawn between the two sets of proceedings and that what we are concerned with here is the proof or disproof of five specific and concrete allegations which have been presented in an order which we made. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In this part of the proceedings, my legal advisor will take over as Defence counsel, and he will be asking the questions, with all due respect, because in our system, we're used to dealing with direct questions and direct answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: There's no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I should ask in Serbian, Your Honours. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You will speak in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I think I can hear you now, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, I see. The translation is coming along now. Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you have said that you called Mr. Vujin by telephone regarding Radic's statement and you spoke with Radic. Do you remember the time when you made the call and do you remember where Mr. Vujin was at that time? Where did you reach him by telephone?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not recall. I think that he was in his office, but he could have possibly responded on his cell phone. I'm not sure. Sometimes I used his mobile phone in order to get in touch with him and sometimes I would call him at the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you properly yesterday, besides Mr. Radic, you also talked with Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he also tell you about what he did or what other persons did at the posts that they were occupying?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: They both talked in contacts with all of us. They didn't talk only to me. They talked to all the detainees and the guards. However, Kvocka was pretty restrained as far as these matters were concerned. Radic talked much more about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ask Mr. Kvocka to write a statement for you too?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask, after talking with Mr. Vujin. There was talk about that. I thought that both of them would provide statements; however, Kvocka refused. He said that he would see what the procedure was and that he needed to consult with his attorneys, something to that effect, and that he was prepared, in any case, to do something about this. He wasn't really precise about who he would consult, whether it would be Vujin or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So both of them did give a statement to Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't my idea to give the statements, in principle, to Mr. Vujin -- Mr. Livingston, but this was always one of the difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Why was it your idea to have the statements given to Mr. Livingston and not to the counsel in chief, Mr. Vujin?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was dissatisfied with the answers and the questions that were posed to these people, and Mr. Livingston was dissatisfied too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you explain why you did not call Mr. Livingston to take the statements from Radic and Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: The procedure was that the counsel in chief had to submit a request to the Tribunal, and the consent of the counsel in chief of those people was also required. I think at that time Mr. Guberina was the attorney for Radic, and Mr. Simic was the attorney for Kvocka. These were the people who cooperated closely with Mr. Vujin from before, especially regarding my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, this probably refers to the request for an official statement with the consent of the attorney and the Court, but I assume that you got the statement outside of this procedure?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But why not with Mr. Livingston? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the true reason was. This was a spontaneous matter. I was surprised that these two were speaking so openly about the events in Prijedor. It's true that the two of them later changed their opinion, but this was my first impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your statement of November 24th, you mentioned the dissatisfaction of Mr. Wladimiroff and your own dissatisfaction with the fact that Mr. Vujin visited some witnesses who had already been interviewed by Mr. Wladimiroff. Could you please tell us what the names of these witnesses were and what Mr. Vujin questioned these witnesses about in that procedure?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, not only then, but later it became clear -- well, I didn't know what kind of conversations he had with these people, but I know for certain that always before Wladimiroff went out in the field of Republika Srpska, he would visit the same witnesses who were supposed to be interviewed by Mr. Wladimiroff, and he said that was his style of work. The proceedings were almost over, and I saw in a videotape where Mr. Vujin was quarrelling with the interpreter for Mr. Wladimiroff, and he was trying to suggest to a lady what she was supposed to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that he had interviewed them after the interviews by Mr. Wladimiroff, and this is how he influenced his strategy?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he would interview them before and after. After, these were people who acted according to the instructions of Mr. Vujin, and these were the investigators Drazic and Kostic who made a series of statements who had already talked with Mr. Wladimiroff. Then Mr. Orie sent a fax for this practice to stop. I think Mr. Livingston was the one who sent this fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We're talking about the period when Mr. Wladimiroff was your counsel in chief, and Mr. Livingston at that time was not on your Defence team, so it's impossible that he sent that fax.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Livingston did send that fax, and I know about that, but it's true that Mr. Livingston was -- Mr. Wladimiroff --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter finds that the pace is too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet and Mr. Tadic, will you both slow down a little for the interpreters? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please tell us now what the names of these witnesses are?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I think at that time Mr. Vujin had already talked to Jadranka Gavranovic, that he had contacts with people such as Jankovic, Sigara Danovic. I can't remember all of them at this time, but I know that such contacts existed and I know that my brother had seen them together at that time over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were these witnesses also interviewed by Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, some were and some were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your letter of November 24th, you stated that you and Mr. Wladimiroff were expressly dissatisfied and found fault with Mr. Vujin because the list of the witnesses, which you claim in this letter was strictly confidential, was well-known to Simo Drljaca and that you believe that this had taken place through the fault of Mr. Vujin. Do you know who the list of witnesses was sent to by Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was given to Mr. Vujin to look at and to no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you look at document or letter 240, 238, 239, and 240? This is a fax, sent by Mr. Wladimiroff to Mr. Vujin, requesting that this list of witnesses be presented to attorney Krstan Simic and to your brothers, with proof on the last page that this was done. It was sent to your brothers and to attorney Krstan Simic. It does not state anywhere that this is strictly confidential, which you stated.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether this is the letter that I have here before me, August 29th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So what do you want to say? Well, this is an instruction for this list, which you claim is strictly confidential, be also delivered to attorney Krstan Simic and your brothers.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was not the same list of witnesses that I'm talking about, that Mr. Wladimiroff had seen in the hands of Mr. Drljaca. These are the names of the members of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could we show the original to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, is there a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it seems, Your Honours, that we don't have copies, but we will make copies if this is possible. Some pages are missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You proceed. (Trial Chamber confers).

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I may be allowed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I am advised by the legal officer that the document appearing at page 240 was accepted by the Appeals Chamber but that two other documents associated with that first document were not accepted, not being in one of the two working languages of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you permit me just to give one explanation. It seems to me that what we were afraid of would happen, there has been a mistake in the fax transmission and there are some pages that are missing, as well as the translation of this text into Serbian. So we request time to prepare this and then we will submit this to the Court in the English language, because this is the list of the witnesses and also the circumstances under which witnesses should testify, with a remark that learned colleague Wladimiroff tried to send by telefax this list to my colleague Mr. Simic and to the brothers. So he asked me to send that. So this is what I did, along with my greetings to Mr. Krstan Simic, to give this fax to the brothers and we will be in touch later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Vujin, we have this practical problem, that the witness is in the box, is being examined on documents which are not accessible to the Tribunal itself. So we can't follow exactly what is being done. That is a problem. I think you'll appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: You're quite right, Your Honours, and we'll withdraw this question and in further proceedings we shall act --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, will you proceed, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me just say that this is not the document which concerns the document given into the hands of Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, could you expect that your Defence counsel would be able to interview witnesses in Prijedor without the knowledge of the authorities of the Republika Srpska, all the more so as they were foreign lawyers who had come with the intention of doing so?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know which period you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The time in Prijedor when you said that Drljaca knew that the witnesses would be questioned, and that this surprised Mr. Wladimiroff, and that this effected co-operation with Mr. Vujin.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, up to that contact with Drljaca, had already interviewed a considerable number of witnesses without anybody's assistance, except the members of my family. Mr. Drljaca and the local authorities did not always have an insight into that. Mr. Wladimiroff really did have problems, but he always personally, via my brothers, was able to come into contact with a number of witnesses who perhaps didn't play an important role at the time. That was precisely the reason and the attempt made by Mr. Wladimiroff. When everybody went back, they were not satisfied with the work of the investigating organs, Kostic and Drazic, and they said, "We'll all go together." This took place prior to the beginning of my Court case, that is to say, in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you explain to us why the witness were not invited to testify?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Which witnesses could you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The ones you say were not able to be interviewed before the trial.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: A number of key witnesses Mr. Wladimiroff was never able to contact. It was precisely for that reason that he tried by legal means to reach them during his last day in the Republika Srpska. That is why he considered and I considered this was a confidential document with key witnesses that we had agreed upon here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You state in your statement that there was a campaign by the authorities in Prijedor and the Republika Srpska against you. Many of the Defence witnesses who are already on the Tribunal's list decided not to testify, and that for that reason no eyewitnesses testified for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is one of the reasons, and the campaign that was launched against me concerned the authorities over there who, in a strange way, proclaimed me in public as a deserter. This was found to be sufficient reason to prohibit anybody to co-operate with my defence. There was an ongoing war on the territory of Republika Srpska at the time, and if you were labelled a deserter, that was much worse than it would have been in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you say that you and Mr. Wladimiroff took offence when you found that some of your witnesses were called to the police station in Prijedor for questioning before they came to testify in The Hague. You found this insulting. Could you explain what this has to do with Mr. Vujin and the notice of appeal that you filed?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was a confidential list of witnesses which Mr. Vujin personally gave to Mr. Drljaca for him to take a look at the list and, for example, a protected Witness U or Q, and even Witness W, were called for questioning. Nobody else could have known who those individuals were before looking at the witness list which included their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, we'll go back to that list of witnesses later on. You state, furthermore, that the statements that Mr. Vujin took from the witnesses and prepared were simple and written in a non-professional way, and that the main characteristic of those statements was that no names of other individuals were mentioned and that the statements just said that you were not present. Can you tell us what the witnesses (sic) looked like that Mr. Livingston took from the witnesses? Did they contain the names of these individuals? Did they contain statements whereby these individuals stated that they had done the acts that you had been charged with here?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us which statements and which witnesses?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first statement given by Miroslav Tadic to Mrs. Sajcic states the names of individuals. In practically all the statements by Mrs. Jadranka, when she questioned them exclusively in the presence of Mr. Livingston, without anybody else's presence, all the details are stipulated, the names of the individuals and the positions they held in Omarska. She just did not dare give names referring to the events in Kozarac, because her life would have been endangered had she stated the names of those individuals, and that is why she called for protective measures in disclosing those facts. But Mr. Livingston knows what she told him orally. I could go on to enumerate several other witnesses but I think that is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, we'll have a chance of looking into that. Can you tell us how it came about that Mr. Livingston became one of the Defence counsels in this case?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can. After the first -- after Mr. Vujin had taken over the defence and his promises given to me, I became convinced that some things were not proceeding as they should be proceeding, and I began to doubt everything that he had promised me. Then I made contact with Mr. Livingston, and that is how he came to be part of my Defence team. So Mr. Vujin had no influence on the engagement of Mr. Livingston as my Defence counsel and they did not know each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us who -- I take it did you not know Mr. Livingston yourself. So who advised you to contact Mr. Livingston?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: These are consultations that I had with members of my family, and they presented their views as to their wishes with regard to Mr. Vujin, particularly in a situation whereby Mr. Kostic, who at the time was to have become a member of the team or had already become a member of my team, refused to go into the field to investigate because he was afraid of the people there. When he heard the people he was to co-operate with, he knew that they were very dangerous and didn't dare to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, in your statement with regard to the questioning of the witnesses in Prijedor, you say that Mr. Milan Vujin unexpectedly became engaged in this process, in the questioning of the witnesses. I'll repeat the question. I seem to have been speaking too fast. You state in your statement that Milan Vujin unexpectedly became included in the preparations with regard to the questioning of potential Defence witnesses. What does that mean when you say that your lead counsel unexpectedly became involved in preparations for the questioning of the witnesses when you say that you had precisely engaged him on the case because you needed him to find the witnesses and question them, witnesses that you thought to be of advantage to you?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: His engagement at the beginning, that is to say -- he always said that there were no problems, that I would have the necessary number of witnesses, the concrete persons that I had stipulated, and there was no question of any order at the time from the International Tribunal that this be effected. What you're talking about now is something that occurred later on when it transpired that I, in fact, had no key witnesses for my defence. When I and Mr. Livingston worked on requesting the Tribunal to help us in this regard, and the people that I myself and Mr. Livingston considered to be important and witnesses that could influence the proceedings here. So Mr. Livingston, at the beginning, was against this type of communication. He said that he had this under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, in your statement, you say that you express dissatisfaction with the work of Mr. Vujin with regard to the taking of statements from witnesses in Prijedor, and you did not then, nor did you now, express your dissatisfaction with Mr. Livingston, although you probably know that Mr. Livingston attended the taking of statements from the witnesses. Both were present, Mr. Livingston and Mr. Vujin. Usually it was Mr. Livingston who took those statements. So how do you explain that you are not satisfied with those statements and that you just criticise Mr. Vujin for that and not Mr. Livingston?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: The statements taken by Mr. Livingston alone in his investigation processes are high-quality statements and represent the kind of statements that I expected to be taken. But the ones you are talking about, these were statements taken in the presence of Mr. Vujin exclusively, and in the presence of an important person from the Serbian organs, and the statements taken at the police station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You state that Mr. Livingston was able to travel to other entities within Bosnia-Herzegovina and that he availed himself of those opportunities, and that in doing so he took statements from other witnesses that were not of Serb ethnicity and that that was an advantage. Can you tell us whether he took statements of this kind, whether those statements were beneficial to you? Could you use them and did you use them?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us what witnesses these were?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Livingston effected these contacts without any consultation with Mr. Vujin, regardless -- that is, he took statements from Hukanovic, for example, in Sanski Most, and I consider that that was a very good statement. He took another statement in Holland from Mr. Hrnic. That too was a very good high-quality statement. He also took a statement from Jadranka Gavranovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We were talking about the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Some of these people said that they would be willing to make their statements exclusively abroad. For example, they had decided to go to London or some neutral city because witnesses said they would be prepared to give these statements only in these neutral places. One of these was Hilmija. I forget her surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were these statements taken?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: A statement was taken from Hukanovic. We had planned to take statements from others. From Hrgic a statement was taken abroad. I can't remember other the others but there are several statements of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were these statements used in the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say "good statements" or "high-quality statements," what do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I mean that questions were asked relevant to my defence and vital facts were raised, facts that I wanted to show this Tribunal and that could have had an important influence on the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did these statements say what these individuals had done and state the names of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Some of these people were victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Regardless of whether they mentioned people and what they did?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, these statements did contain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Vujin questioned witness Danicic at all?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see that statement?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did and I tore it up. I tore it up in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And that statement was not used?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had a copy and whether he gave anything else to the Tribunal, because as I say, I didn't have any insight in what he did convey to the Tribunal, but I was angry because it had tipped the bucket. It was just too much. In addition to all the evidence that was in existence, he worked as he had always worked previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know whether Milorad Tadic, nicknamed Brka was questioned?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, by Mr. Livingston on several occasions. That was an individual who gave very valuable data related to everything that took place in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mean in that statement?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Some of those facts were in the statement, others he gave personally. That is something that facilitated the investigation led by Mr. Livingston. So there were some facts given orally which he did not dare give in writing because he feared for his life, and particularly because Mr. Vujin had insight into some of the statements. So Mr. Milorad himself stated that Mr. Vujin was working contrary to my interests. I was not sure of that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, did Mr. Tadic (sic) take a statement from witness Saponja?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Has that statement been tendered?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember its contents?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know which version was submitted. There were two versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say there were two versions? There were two statements?

utterances.speaker: Dusko Tadic (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that's the problem and that's what I mentioned a moment ago. Mr. Vujin took one statement which he showed here to the Tribunal in The Hague, and in the same way, once again the questions were not asked relating to the facts vital to my defence, and I expressed my open dissatisfaction. He said there were no problems. He said he would take the statement again from that particular individual. Later on he showed me the second statement, and it contained practically the same things that the first statement contained. It was a little expanded, but what was the strangest thing was the date was the same, and the first two pages were the same, and it was only the last page that was slightly different. So I was no longer certain whether actually two statements had been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember the contents of the statement, something that would be important, in your mind?
